# Sif: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Sif** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Shearing of the Golden Hair.** Loki Laufeyjarson, Snorri begins, did this for mischief: he cut off all Sif's hair.  When Þórr came home and learned it, he seized Loki and would have broken every bone in him, had Loki not sworn to go to the svartálfar and have them make for Sif a head of hair from gold — hair that would grow like other hair.  So Loki went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi, and they made the hair, and it grew to her head the moment it was set there, as if it were her own.

**The Wager That Forged Mjölnir.** The sons of Ívaldi did not stop at the hair: in the same commission they made Gungnir, the spear that never misses, for [[odinn|Óðinn]], and Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, for [[freyr|Freyr]].  Then Loki wagered his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three treasures as good.  In the forge Sindri laid gold, a boar's hide, and iron in the fire in turn, while Loki, in fly-shape, stung the bellows-worker — and out came Draupnir the dripping ring, Gullinbursti the golden-bristled boar, and Mjölnir, the hammer whose handle came short only because the fly stung Brokkr's eyelid at the last draw.

**The Crystal Cup.** In Ægir's hall, as Loki works down the company with slander and no one escapes — not the serving-woman Fimafengr, not the gods' wives — Sif alone rises and pours him mead in a crystal cup, and speaks the flyting's one courteous stanza: 'Hail to thee, Loki, and take the crystal cup, full of ancient mead; so may you say that I alone, among the Æsir's kin, am without blame. ' It is a bid for exemption, gracefully made, by the one person in the hall who tries hospitality instead of abuse. Loki's answer is the flyting's coldest stroke: he grants she would be blameless indeed, wary and shy of men, were it not that he knows one who lay with her and drew the mighty Þórr's wife from home — 'and that was I, wretched one.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves


## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Sif

- **Meaning:** "Relation by marriage"

- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᛋᛁᚠ
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 328 of 397

## The Name Travels

Sif has attracted exactly one great comparative reading, and it begins with her hair.  Jacob Grimm, in the Deutsche Mythologie, took the shearing and the golden regrowth as a nature myth: Sif's hair is the ripe corn, Loki's shearing the harvest or the blight, and the dwarfs' gold the field that grows back golden — a reading that made her a Germanic harvest-goddess beside Demeter and the corn-mothers of folklore, and that matches the way the corpus ties her to Þórr, the farmer's weather-god.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Sif** stands at [/sites/sif/](/sites/sif/) — [lore](/sites/sif/lore/), [scholars](/sites/sif/scholars/), [patterns](/sites/sif/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.
